chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Al-Hasan ibn Mahboub, from Ibn Bukayr and Ali ibn Ri'ab, from Zurara ibn A'yan, who said:

I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about a man who married a woman in Iraq, then went to Syria and married another woman, who turned out to be the sister of the woman in Iraq. He (peace be upon him) said: He is separated from the one he married in Syria, and he does not approach her until the waiting period of the Syrian woman expires.

I said: What if he married a woman, then married her mother, while he did not know that she was her mother? He (peace be upon him) said: Allah has excused his ignorance in that. Then he (peace be upon him) said: When he knows that she is her mother, he should not approach her, nor approach the daughter, until the mother's waiting period expires from him. So when the mother's waiting period expires, the marriage with the daughter becomes permissible for him.
I said: What if the mother gives birth to a child? He (peace be upon him) said: It is his child, and it will be his son, and the brother of his wife.

key_terms.جَهَالَتُهُ: His ignorance (excuse for not knowing the prohibited relationship)
key_terms.عِدَّةُ: Iddah (waiting period for a woman after divorce or death of husband)
key_terms.يُفَرَّقُ: Separation (divorce or separation of conjugal rights)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a man marrying two sisters or a mother and daughter simultaneously in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi elucidates the jurisprudential nuances of 'jam' al-ukhtayn' (gathering two sisters) and 'jam' al-umm wa al-bint' (mother and daughter), emphasizing the distinction between the prohibition of consummation and the validity of the marriage contract. It highlights the Shia principle of 'jahalah' (ignorance) exempting the husband from penalty during the waiting period ('iddah') of the second wife, ensuring legal clarity for offspring legitimacy. The ruling underscores the procedural requirement to wait for the expiration of the 'iddah' of the newly revealed relative before consummating the marriage with the first, reflecting a careful balance between marital rights and kinship prohibitions.
